requirements.requirement: Traffic node3 sends to node4 on TCP/8080 is steered across the first transit network
requirements.summary: VyOS PBR rule 10 matches TCP dport 8080 into table 108 routing via eth1 (transit1). Live tcpdump captures on node1 eth1 during a real curl from node3 show the complete SYN-through-FIN 8080 exchange, with zero 8080 packets appearing on eth2. Re-confirmed after full four-node reboot cycle (11 tagged 8080 packets on eth1, 0 on eth2).

requirements.requirement: Traffic node3 sends to node4 on TCP/9090 is steered across the second transit network
requirements.summary: VyOS PBR rule 20 matches TCP dport 9090 into table 109 routing via eth2 (transit2). tcpdump on node1 eth2 shows the complete 9090 SYN-through-FIN exchange with zero 9090 packets on eth1, confirmed both before and after the full reboot cycle.

requirements.requirement: Both the 8080 and 9090 flows actually reach node4
requirements.summary: curl from node3 to node4 (10.10.22.2) returns HTTP 200 on both port 8080 and port 9090, confirmed at multiple points including after the full sequential reboot of all four nodes.

requirements.requirement: Show which transit network carried each flow
requirements.summary: Simultaneous, interface-tagged tcpdump captures on node1 (eth1=transit1, eth2=transit2) directly demonstrate exclusive separation of the two flows, both pre- and post-reboot, with packet-count summaries (11 8080 packets on eth1, 11 9090 packets on eth2, zero cross-contamination).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on every managed node (baseline, restart ack, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/cluster state)
requirements.summary: All four nodes show a complete transition: pre-restart healthy baseline (boot_id/kern.boottime plus working curl or config), an explicit reboot acknowledgement, a directly observed changed post-restart boot identity, and recovered routing/firewall/PBR configuration confirmed functionally via successful cross-node curl retests. This is cross-checked and consistent with the fixed after-prepare/after-executor lifecycle snapshots, which independently show all four boot identities changed. node4's ad-hoc python HTTP test listeners (not part of the task, purely executor test tooling) were not persisted and were manually restarted post-reboot, which is a reasonable and disclosed limitation rather than a task defect.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material outcomes of the task: TCP/8080 and TCP/9090 traffic from node3 to node4 are steered via distinct, verified transit paths (VyOS policy-based routing plus OPNsense route-to/reply-to pf rules), both flows successfully reach node4 (HTTP 200), and simultaneous per-interface tcpdump captures directly and repeatedly demonstrate which transit network carried each flow, both before and after a full sequential reboot of all four nodes. The independent provider-wide restart-evidence protocol is also satisfied for all four nodes with coherent baseline/ack/changed-identity/recovered-functional evidence, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. Hygiene is good overall: iterative topology discovery and pf-rule refinement were bounded and superseded, one duplicate-IP mistake was self-corrected, and only minor uncleaned temp-file residue remains on node3/node4.
limitations: node4's HTTP test servers (python3 http.server) were ad-hoc executor test tooling, not a task requirement, and were not persisted across reboot — they required manual restart, which is disclosed but is a minor gap in an otherwise complete restart-evidence chain.

Small residual temp files (/tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/pingout.log, /tmp/srv8080.log, /tmp/srv9090.log) were left on node3 and node4 and not cleaned up, unlike node1/node2 which had explicit cleanup commands.

OPNsense pf pass rules on opt1/opt2/opt3 are broader ('inet all') than the two specific ports required by the task; this appears necessary for bidirectional PBR/reply-to correctness in this topology rather than an unrelated security weakening, but it is a wider exposure than a port-scoped rule would be.

Requirement provider-wide-node-restart-evidence cited unknown evidence IDs: global:after_prepare:node1:boot-identity, global:after_prepare:node2:boot-identity, global:after_prepare:node3:boot-identity, global:after_prepare:node4:boot-identity

operational_hygiene.summary: The executor performed a reasonable amount of hands-on topology discovery via trial IP assignment on node1/node2 interfaces (e.g. cmd-8be46033426e452f, cmd-92c9b149cf2145aa, cmd-b3201ffebf194423, cmd-4af3fce204b14bec cycling through several throwaway subnets before settling on 10.10.21/31/32), which is bounded, low-risk, and fully superseded by the final persisted config — acceptable discovery given the task did not specify exact physical wiring. One self-corrected mistake occurred: node4 and node2 were briefly both assigned 10.10.22.1 (cmd-acc736de0cc14061 vs cmd-37c0bc804c444033/cmd-cd5b9744bec6447c), caught via failed ARP resolution and fixed without lasting effect. OPNsense pf rules were iterated multiple times (route-to, then reply-to via gateway auto-assignment) via base64-piped python edits to config.xml (cmd-23336d4115024972, cmd-12e9a26d12634c9d, cmd-ab9be3a0819e4678, cmd-94e656abd6e64cf5) — this was necessary iterative refinement to get asymmetric routing/reply-to correct, not unrelated churn, though the resulting 'pass in quick ... inet all' rules on opt1/opt2/opt3 are broader than strictly needed for only ports 8080/9090; this is a minor, low-risk permissiveness intrinsic to enabling bidirectional PBR through-routing rather than a genuine security downgrade of pre-existing controls. Temp-file cleanup was performed on node1 and node2 (cmd-4c9ea1c917b848a9, cmd-b793c72b1e084a97, cmd-8d995fde3010457f) but not on node3/node4, leaving small residual files (/tmp/pingout.log, /tmp/reboot.log on node3; /tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/srv8080.log, /tmp/srv9090.log on node4) visible in the after-executor lifecycle snapshot — minor, non-destructive residue.
